text: What do you believe about how to live, that you have not chosen but inherited?
evaluation: Inheritance is not refutation, but unexamined inheritance often is. The question opens the audit.

text: What do you believe about how to live, that you have chosen against the people who raised you?
evaluation: Some chosen beliefs are growth; some are reaction. Tell them apart by asking whether the belief survives without the family it pushes against.

text: What is one belief you hold that you cannot defend, but will not surrender?
evaluation: Indefensible-but-held beliefs are honest territory. Mark them; don't apologise for them; don't pretend they're arguments.

text: What is one belief you defend in public that you doubt in private?
evaluation: Public-private mismatch is corrosive over time. Either align or admit the mismatch to yourself first.

text: What kind of person do you become when no one is watching?
evaluation: The honest answer is the test. Many people are kinder unwatched than watched; some are crueller. Both deserve attention.

text: What kind of person do you become when you are sure you will be remembered for what you do next?
evaluation: Counterpart. The audience self and the unwatched self are both yours. The ethical work is closing the gap.

text: What is the right amount of time to spend thinking about your own death this year?
evaluation: Honest answer is rarely zero. The question itself is therapeutic for many.

text: What is the wrong amount of time you spent thinking about your own death last year, and what was it about?
evaluation: Either too much or too little. The pattern under the time is the question.

text: What would you want said about you at your funeral, that you have not yet earned?
evaluation: The eulogy gap. Force specifics; the work is in closing the gap, not perfecting the wish.

text: What would be said about you at your funeral, if those who knew you best spoke without filter?
evaluation: The unfiltered eulogy is often kinder than feared and more specific than hoped. Worth imagining.

text: What is one question you do not want answered before you die?
evaluation: Some not-knowing is sacred. Naming it protects it.

text: What is one question you very much want answered before you die, and what would it cost you to seek it?
evaluation: If the question is real, the cost is usually less than the not-knowing. If you are not paying, examine why.

text: What does meaningful work mean to you, in a sentence with no abstractions?
evaluation: Force concreteness. 'Reduces a specific suffering, builds a specific thing, teaches a specific person' beats 'makes a difference'.

text: What does meaningless work look like to you, that you have made peace with doing?
evaluation: Most lives include meaningless work. The peace, when honest, is healthier than the rage.

text: What is one thing you do that you secretly believe is sacred?
evaluation: Often small: making coffee, walking a route, tucking in a child. The secret is the marker of sacredness.

text: What is one thing you treat as sacred that, examined, may not be?
evaluation: Some sacreds are habit dressed up. Audit gently.

text: What is one ethical line you have crossed that you can name now without shame?
evaluation: Without shame is the test. Naming with shame still keeps it underground; naming without shame integrates it.

text: What is one ethical line you held when crossing would have been easier, and what did the holding cost you?
evaluation: Cost of integrity is usually denied. Naming the price honours the choice.

text: What does forgiveness mean to you, in concrete behaviour?
evaluation: Force concreteness. 'Letting it go' is a result, not a behaviour. The behaviour is closer to ceasing to rehearse.

text: What is one thing you have not yet forgiven, and what would forgiving it cost the part of you that holds it?
evaluation: Resentment is sometimes structural. The held grudge costs something to release; that cost is real.

text: What is one thing you have forgiven yourself for, and what made the forgiveness possible?
evaluation: Self-forgiveness is rarer than forgiveness of others, and harder to fake. Notice the conditions.

text: What is one thing you have not yet forgiven yourself for, and what is the part of you that won't let it go?
evaluation: The unwilling part often deserves a hearing, not an argument.

text: What is one place where your beliefs and your behaviour disagree, and which is winning?
evaluation: Behaviour usually wins. Either change the behaviour or revise the belief; the gap itself is corrosive.

text: What is one place where your behaviour is ahead of your stated belief, and what does the behaviour know that the belief hasn't admitted?
evaluation: Sometimes practice precedes belief. The body is wiser than the slogan.

text: What is one inherited religious or moral instruction that turned out to be useful, even after you stopped believing the framing?
evaluation: Useful without true is a coherent stance. Saves overthrowing the practical with the theoretical.

text: What is one inherited religious or moral instruction that turned out to be harmful, that you have not finished unlearning?
evaluation: Unlearning is slow. Name the residue; don't pretend the instruction is fully gone.

text: What does a good death look like to you, for yourself?
evaluation: Not morbid. Knowing the picture orients many small daily decisions.

text: What does a good death look like to you, for the people you love?
evaluation: Often informs how to be present in their late life. The picture is a gift to give.

text: What is one regret you carry that you have stopped trying to fix, and have started trying to live with?
evaluation: Some regrets are unfixable. Living with them is the work, not solving them.

text: What is one regret you carry that, on examination, may yet be addressable?
evaluation: Some regrets are still open. Make the call. Send the letter. Show up.

text: What is one truth about your life you have been waiting to be ready for?
evaluation: Readiness is rarely the actual obstacle. The truth is. Naming it is the move.

text: What is one truth about your life you have been pretending you are not ready for, that you actually are?
evaluation: Counterpart. Strategic delay disguised as readiness work.

text: What does dignity mean to you, when you have least of it?
evaluation: Sickness, poverty, public failure. The definition under stress is the real definition.

text: What does dignity mean to you, when you have most of it?
evaluation: Counterpart. Some forms of dignity only become visible in plenty; others only in lack. Both are yours.

text: What is one thing you would do differently if you knew you had ten years to live?
evaluation: Concrete answer beats abstract. Then ask: what is stopping the change now?

text: What is one thing you would do differently if you knew you had thirty years to live?
evaluation: Different horizon, different answer. Both shape the present.

text: What is one thing you would not change, even with ten years left?
evaluation: The kept things are the actual core. Useful to know.

text: What is the question you would ask your dying self, and what do you imagine the answer would be?
evaluation: The imagined answer is often closer to truth than the present-day rationalisation.

text: What does loyalty to the truth cost you, in your current life?
evaluation: Friendships, jobs, comfort. The cost should be nameable; if zero, examine the loyalty.

text: What does loyalty to comfort cost you, in your current life?
evaluation: Counterpart. Comfort has its own bill. Pay attention.

text: What is one thing you suspect about reality that you have been afraid to take seriously?
evaluation: Spiritual, philosophical, scientific, political. The suspicion is data; the avoidance is more data.

text: What is one thing you assert about reality that you have been afraid to question seriously?
evaluation: Counterpart. Some asserted certainties are armour. Permission to question is its own freedom.

text: What is the kind of suffering you most want to reduce, in the world or in your own house?
evaluation: Specific suffering. Specific reduction. Big abstractions are usually evasions.

text: What is the kind of suffering you have grown numb to, that you would not be proud of?
evaluation: Numbness is honest, not virtuous. Naming it is the first step away from it.

text: What is one act of courage from your past that, in retrospect, was easier than it felt?
evaluation: Useful for re-calibration. Some 'courage' was just doing the thing once the moment forced it.

text: What is one act of cowardice from your past that, in retrospect, was harder to overcome than you knew at the time?
evaluation: Generosity to the past self. The hard moments deserve credit even when they ended in failure.

text: What is one practice that has actually changed who you are, over years?
evaluation: Reading, walking, prayer, therapy, parenting, weight training, writing. Specific. Real changes are slow and visible.

text: What is one practice you keep that, honestly, has not changed you, and what does that tell you?
evaluation: Either change the practice or release it. Identity-rituals without effect are expensive.

text: What is one teacher or text that genuinely changed how you think, and how do you know?
evaluation: The 'how do you know' separates real influence from name-dropping.

text: What is one teacher or text you cite, that you suspect did not actually change you?
evaluation: Citation as decoration is common. Honesty here is freeing.

text: What is one piece of beauty in the world you would walk a long way to see again?
evaluation: Specific place, sound, person, moment. The pull is data about what your life is for.

text: What is one piece of beauty in your own life you have stopped noticing, that you would miss instantly if it left?
evaluation: Re-noticing is a small practice with large effects.

text: What is one fear you have stopped pretending isn't there?
evaluation: Naming a fear shrinks it without dispelling it. The shrinkage is enough to act.

text: What is one fear you are still pretending isn't there, that may run more of your life than you admit?
evaluation: The denied fear often shapes the most decisions. Surface gently.

text: What is one inheritance — material, emotional, cultural — you have not yet decided what to do with?
evaluation: Undecided inheritances accumulate. Decide once, gently.

text: What is one inheritance you have decided to refuse, and what does the refusal cost?
evaluation: Refusal costs relationship, sometimes. The cost should be examined; not all refusals are wise, not all are unwise.

text: What is one form of love you have received that you are still learning to recognise as love?
evaluation: Often: discipline, distance, restraint, refusal. Late recognition is real recognition.

text: What is one form of love you have given that the recipient could not recognise as love?
evaluation: Counterpart. Sometimes the form is wrong; sometimes the recipient. Differentiate.

text: What does freedom mean to you, today, that it did not mean ten years ago?
evaluation: Definitions evolve. The tracking is the work.

text: What does freedom mean to you, today, that it will probably not mean ten years from now?
evaluation: Forecast the next revision. Knowing the impermanence of the current definition holds it lightly.

text: What is one obligation in your life that, on examination, is actually a choice you keep making?
evaluation: Disguised choices are common. Re-recognising them as choices restores agency.

text: What is one choice in your life that, on examination, is actually an obligation you should honour?
evaluation: Counterpart. Some 'I choose this' framings hide debts that deserve to be acknowledged.

text: What is one promise you have made to your future self that you are still keeping?
evaluation: Catalogue. Kept promises to self are the bedrock of self-trust.

text: What is one promise you have made to your future self that you have quietly broken?
evaluation: Either renew the promise, replace it, or release it. Quietly broken promises silently corrode.

text: What does it mean to live a good life, in the most boring, most honest sentence you can write?
evaluation: Boring beats poetic. The sentence should be one you could say at the kitchen table.

text: What does it mean to live a wasted life, in the most boring, most honest sentence you can write?
evaluation: Counterpart. Knowing the contour of waste sharpens the contour of good.

text: What is one part of your life that, looking back, you will probably call wasted?
evaluation: Honest answer beats absolution. Sometimes the answer is no part. Sometimes it's a decade. Both are real.

text: What is one part of your life that, looking back, you will probably call essential, that you do not yet recognise as essential?
evaluation: The unsung middle. Caregiving, recovery, quiet years. Often the actual ground.

text: What is one act of generosity that returned to you in a form you did not expect?
evaluation: Notice. The pattern, repeated, becomes a stance toward the world.

text: What is one act of generosity that did not return, and what is your relationship to that ledger?
evaluation: Generosity that requires return is exchange. The ledger answer reveals the actual stance.

text: What is one truth about money you wish you had absorbed at twenty?
evaluation: Specific, lived truth. Save it for someone twenty now.

text: What is one truth about money you wish you could un-absorb, that runs your decisions?
evaluation: Scarcity beliefs from childhood, status anxieties, parental scripts. Naming the script is half the freedom.

text: What does enough look like, for you, in numbers, with no flourishes?
evaluation: If you cannot name the number, you cannot reach it. The number is allowed to be wrong; refusing to write it is the cost.

text: What would you do the day after you reached enough, that you are not doing now?
evaluation: The honest answer often reveals that the current trade is not for the money, but for the avoidance of what enough would require.

text: What is one moment in your life where time genuinely stopped, that you can return to in memory at will?
evaluation: Anchor moments. They orient the rest of the life.

text: What is one moment that should have stopped time, that you barely noticed at the time?
evaluation: Late seeing. The recognition is itself a form of presence delivered to the past.

text: What is one place that holds you, even when you are not in it?
evaluation: Concrete place. The holding is portable; carry it.

text: What is one place you have left that, if you returned, would no longer hold you the same way?
evaluation: Some homes are stages of life, not coordinates. Honest grief without bitterness.

text: What does it mean to be a good ancestor, for the people you will not meet?
evaluation: Long-time horizon. The answer often constrains short-time choices in clarifying ways.

text: What does it mean to be a bad ancestor, in a small, ordinary way?
evaluation: The small ways are the ways. Catastrophic ancestor-failure is rare; ordinary ancestor-failure is constant.

text: What is one thing you used to think was wisdom, that you now think was just survival?
evaluation: The reclassification matters. Survival deserves credit but not generalisation.

text: What is one thing you used to think was just survival, that you now recognise was wisdom?
evaluation: Counterpart. Some old strategies aged into wisdom. Notice them. Honour them.

text: What is one thing you would tell your younger self, if you knew the younger self could hear it without arguing?
evaluation: The 'without arguing' clause filters the lecture. What you would actually say, gently.

text: What is one thing your younger self would tell you, that you would have to listen to without arguing?
evaluation: Counterpart. Often the harder direction.

text: What does it mean, to you, to die well, in the ordinary sense — not heroic, just decent?
evaluation: Decent dying is more available than heroic dying. Knowing the picture relaxes the present.

text: What kind of pain are you willing to carry for the rest of your life, because it belongs to a love you will not surrender?
evaluation: Old grief, ongoing care, consequence of a chosen path. Naming the carriage is honouring it.

text: What kind of pain are you carrying that you suspect does not belong to you, that you could set down?
evaluation: Counterpart. Inherited or absorbed pain that is not yours to keep. The setting-down is a real practice.

text: What is the prayer you say, even if you do not pray, when something matters?
evaluation: Inner sentence under stress. Reveals what one actually believes when the polite frame falls.

text: What is the prayer you used to say, that you have stopped saying, and what filled the space?
evaluation: Replacement matters. Atheism is sometimes a substitution; sometimes a clearing. Both are real.

text: What does it mean to belong somewhere, when no place fits?
evaluation: Diasporic, displaced, queer, neuro-divergent, mixed-heritage lives produce real answers here. Honour them.

text: What does it mean to belong somewhere, when many places almost fit?
evaluation: Counterpart. Multi-belonging carries its own costs and its own grace.

text: What is one truth about other people you have stopped trying to forgive them for?
evaluation: Acceptance without forgiveness is a coherent stance. The forgiveness frame doesn't fit every wound.

text: What is one truth about yourself you have stopped trying to fix, and what changed when you stopped?
evaluation: Acceptance is sometimes the work, not the failure. The change is usually visible to others first.

text: What is one truth about yourself you should still be trying to change, that you have prematurely accepted?
evaluation: Counterpart. Acceptance can be evasion. Tell the differences.

text: What does it mean to live with hope without lying, when honesty would have you despair?
evaluation: The hardest practice. Hope as discipline, not as forecast. The distinction is the work.

text: What does it mean to live with despair without lying, when hope would be the easier social posture?
evaluation: Counterpart. Sometimes the honest stance is grim. Permission to hold it briefly is part of integrity.

text: What is one sentence you want to be able to say truthfully, by the end of this year?
evaluation: Compose the sentence first. Then live toward it. Honest target.

text: What is one sentence you want never to have to say, by the end of this year, and what would prevent you?
evaluation: The avoided sentence reveals the value protected. The prevention is concrete action.

text: What is one thing you understand now that you suspect you will misunderstand again, in a different shape?
evaluation: Humility about the future self. Understandings cycle; humility lets them re-arrive.

text: What is one sentence about how you want to live, that you would want carved somewhere small, where only you would see it?
evaluation: Closing. Small. Private. Real. The sentence is the orientation; carving it makes it harder to forget.
